title: Fix it: validate a record against a schema given as data
prompt:
The script in the editor is **almost** right. It passes on the sample and fails on a case you cannot see.

The original task was:

The payload is `{ schema, record }`. `schema` is an object mapping field names to a rule shaped like `{ kind, required }`, where `kind` is one of `"String"`, `"Number"`, `"Boolean"`, `"Object"`, `"Array"`, and `required` is `true` or `false`.

When `kind` is `"Object"`, the rule also has `fields` — another schema of the same shape, describing `record`'s nested value for that field. When `kind` is `"Array"`, the rule also has `itemKind` — one of the scalar kinds, which every element of the array must match.

Return an array of every violation found anywhere in `record`, as strings, in the form `<path> is required` or `<path> must be a <Kind>`, using a dotted path such as `user.address.city` and a bracketed index such as `tags[1]` for array elements. A field that is missing is only a violation when its rule says it is required. Find every violation, not just the first one for a field and not just the first field with a problem — a record with three things wrong reports all three.

Find what is wrong and fix it. You can press Run to see what it currently does.

cases.output: ["name is required", "age must be a Number"]
["tags[1] must be a String", "tags[3] must be a String"]
["order.id is required", "order.tags[1] must be a String"]

hints: Run it on the sample first. If the sample looks right, the bug only shows on data the sample does not contain.
Ask what kind of input would break this — an empty list, a missing field, a value ordered differently.

declares the pluck callback as (field, rule) instead of (rule, field) — pluck always hands the value first, so `field` is actually bound to the rule object and interpolating it into the path throws immediately

explanation.approach: Each field in the schema resolves to its own small array of errors — empty when that field is fine — and the overall result is every one of those arrays flattened together, so nothing needs a running total that grows as the walk proceeds. `pluck` supplies the `(rule, field)` pairs; for each one, `record[field]` is looked up and tested for missing-when-required, then, if it is present, matched against `rule.kind`. Three of the five kinds are leaves and get checked with `is` directly. The other two are not: `"Object"` means there is a nested schema (`rule.fields`) and a nested value, and `validate` is called again on exactly those, with the path extended by the field's own name; `"Array"` means every element gets checked against `rule.itemKind` and all of those results get flattened in too. The near-miss stops at confirming the field's own container type and never goes back inside it — which behaves identically to the real thing on a schema that happens not to nest, and silently drops every violation that lives one level deeper.

snippets.label: The sample: a missing field and a wrong type, both reported

expect.output: ["name is required", "age must be a Number"]

snippets.note: Two independent problems on two independent fields, both present in the result — neither one stops the walk before the other is found.

snippets.label: An empty schema has nothing to check
snippets.note: `pluck` over an empty object produces nothing to flatten, whatever the record itself contains — there is no rule to hold it to.

snippets.label: Errors from two different nested branches both survive
snippets.note: `user.name` is missing and `user.address.city` is missing two levels down — both come back, with the path built up one field at a time as `validate` calls itself.

snippets.label: The near-miss on that same nested payload: silence
snippets.note: `user` is present and is an Object, so `check` says it's fine and stops — `rule.fields` is never looked at, so the two missing fields inside it are never found.

snippets.label: The same near-miss still catches a top-level type mismatch
snippets.note: This is why the bug ships unnoticed: it is not silent about everything, only about what is nested. A field of the wrong container type at the top level is still caught; it is only the contents of a correctly-typed Object or Array that never get looked at.

snippets.label: Every bad element of an array is reported, not just the first

expect.output: ["tags[1] must be a String", "tags[3] must be a String"]

snippets.note: Index `1` (the number) and index `3` (the boolean) are both wrong, and both come back — `map` runs `check` against every element independently before the results are flattened together.
